competitive_landscape: Busan's waterfront is served today by road, metro and a thin slate of harbour-cruise and conventional ferry operators; the Busan↔Geoje link is essentially a car journey over the Geoga fixed link. On the international corridor, the fast Queen Beetle hydrofoil to Fukuoka was withdrawn at the end of 2024, leaving only slower conventional ferries (Camellia Line and others). Everywhere the pattern is the same: a city defined by water that still moves its people by road or slow diesel boat — exactly the status quo a fast, clean foiling network improves on.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Carries the everyday network: the ~30 nm Busan↔Geoje shipyard line and the short intra-bay Haeundae / Gwangalli / North Port / Yeongdo waterfront hops — all comfortably inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Opens the long international line-haul — Busan↔Fukuoka (~110 nm) and Busan↔Tsushima-range crossings — where the hybrid range and refuel-anywhere model remove any charging-infrastructure dependency on a cross-border route.

regulatory_note: Domestic operations sit under Korea's Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and the Busan Port Authority, aligned with Korea's push toward greener harbour craft and Busan's marine-city / smart-port ambitions. The Busan↔Fukuoka line is an established international ferry corridor with existing immigration/customs terminals on both sides.
seasonality: The South Sea is workable year-round but the East Asian summer brings the typhoon season (roughly Jul–Sep) and the winter NE monsoon raises short steep chop in the open approaches. Foiling above the surface delivers a markedly smoother, more reliable ride in exactly the conditions that slow or cancel conventional craft.

summary: Busan is Korea's second city and one of the world's busiest container ports, wrapped around a string of bays — Haeundae, Gwangalli, North Port — that the city is actively redeveloping into a marine-city waterfront. Just across Jinhae Bay sits Geoje, home to two of the planet's largest shipyards (Samsung Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean) and the executives and engineers who shuttle to them. The water is the most direct line between all of these points, yet today everyone drives the long way round or boards slow diesel craft — the corridor is wide open for a fast, smooth, all-electric link.
tagline: Korea's maritime capital — a 3.3M-person port city, the world's biggest shipyards an hour away by road, and a waterfront begging to be reconnected by water.

use_cases.body: A direct ~30 nm all-electric foiling shuttle between central Busan and the Geoje shipyards replaces the 50-minute bay-circling drive for the executives, classification surveyors, and engineers moving between Busan HQs and the Samsung Heavy / Hanwha Ocean yards.
